title: Rare Association of Leukocytoclastic Vasculitis in Visceral Leishmaniaisis
case_text:
A 30-year-old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and non-itchy, erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low-grade intermittent fever of three-months duration. On examination, the patient was pale and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks [Figure 1]. He was malnourished (body mass index = 18.4 kg/m2), and abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly.
A complete blood count suggested pancytopenia (hemoglobin = 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count = 2800/mm3, and thrombocyte count = 45 000/muL). Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL) was noted with normal liver and renal function tests. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable.
We considered hematological malignancy or a connective tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained were HIV, scrub typhus rickettsia, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Anti-nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative. Urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti-hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative. Peripheral blood antibodies towards rK39 antigen were positive, and bone marrow examination confirmed visceral leishmaniasis with the presence of typical Leishman-Donovan bodies (amastigote form) within the bone marrow histiocytes [Figure 2]. Skin biopsy of the rashes revealed fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall along with extravasation of red blood cells and nuclear debris in the adjoining areas consistent with a diagnosis of leukocytoclastic vasculitis [Figure 3].
Conventional amphotericin B (0.7 mg/kg/day) was given for 14 days with close monitoring of electrolytes, renal function, and urine output along with adequate nutritional support. During treatment, the patient's fever resolved, his blood counts improved, and we noted complete resolution of skin rash.

Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Leishmaniasis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: visceral leishmaniasis associated with leukocytoclastic vasculitis
